Outcome Statement: By 2027, more people in Sri Lanka, particularly the most vulnerable, access and benefit from equitable, resilient, gender-responsive and quality social services with enhanced well-being and dignity.

THEORY OF CHANGE: The pathway of change for this Outcome to be realized requires that:
- The Government at national and subnational levels delivers quality social services (health, food security and nutrition, water, sanitation and hygiene, education, housing, and protection) to all throughout the life cycle, particularly to vulnerable groups, that are more accessible, affordable, equitable, inclusive, gender-responsive and resilient to crises and natural disasters. 
- The Government ensures comprehensive and shock-resilient social protection mechanisms which are more inclusive with expanded coverage.
- Household food security and nutrition is enhanced, particularly for the most vulnerable and households with young children.
- More people have the knowledge, skills and means to demand and actively participate in promoting quality social services for all, particularly those most vulnerable, and to address harmful social norms and practice behaviors which are safe, healthy and protective.

Contributes to SDG Goal 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 10 & 16.

projects.name: Support to the implementation of Sri Lanka's nationally determined contributions in the industry sector
projects.description:
This is a 5-year project funded by the European Union under GCCA+ initiative. The main government counterparts are the Ministry of Industry, Ministry of Environment and the Ministry of Energy and the Ministry of Power.

The overall objective of the Project is to contribute to climate change mitigation through supporting the implementation of Sri Lanka's Nationally Determined Contributions (NDC) for the industrial sector. The specific Project objective is to scale-up the climate change response of Sri Lanka’s industrial sector through the design and implementation of technical, policy, regulatory and financial tools and mechanisms to accelerate the deployment of renewable energy, energy and resource efficiency technologies and best practices.
 
The Project aims to achieve greenhouse gas emission reductions through accelerating the uptake of innovative technologies, established best practices and methods for reducing carbon intensity and improving energy and resource efficiency performance of Sri Lanka’s industrial sector. Furthermore, this project is envisioned to contribute to long-term development gains such as capacity building of the government counterparts and empowerment of the project beneficiaries.
 
 
 
Expected Outcomes:
• EO1: A Monitoring, Review and Verification (MRV) system for the industry sector is developed and implemented and baseline for the industrial sector established
• EO2: An industrial sector plan for implementing NDCs has been validated and activities prioritized according to agreed criteria
• EO3: Policy and regulatory frameworks are improved and related awareness and capacity building of stakeholders to implement these frameworks have been built
• EO4: Capacity related to climate change mitigation practices in the area of industry is built
• EO5: Pilot technologies and methodologies leading to improved energy efficiency and reduction in GHG emissions are tested to be then replicated
 
The Project is implemented with the support of EU GCCA+ initiative, which aims to assist the world’s most vulnerable countries to respond to climate change. The project corresponds with the following priorities: to contribute to enhancing Sri Lanka's resilience to climate change while enabling the engagement in low-carbon development processes via the implementation of the NDCs.

*Actual project start date is 1 January 2022.

projects.name: Inclusive Climate-Smart Dairy Value Chains: Accelerating Renewable Energy Adoption, Nature-Based Solutions, and Smallholder Resilience (1005671)
projects.description:
Sri Lanka’s dairy sector is at a critical juncture, facing cascading climate shocks, economic hardship, and deepening rural inequality—challenges that disproportionately affect women, youth, and marginalized estate communities. Rural poverty has more than doubled since 2019, and women—who make up a significant share of the agricultural workforce—are especially vulnerable due to limited access to resources, technology, and decision-making platforms. In climate-vulnerable districts like Kilinochchi and Nuwara Eliya, smallholder dairy farmers, including women-headed households and aspiring youth agri-entrepreneurs, struggle with declining productivity, input shortages, and nutrition insecurity. The destabilization of the dairy sector threatens household food security, 
particularly for children and women in estate areas where dairy is often the only accessible protein source.

This intervention builds on and represents a continuation of earlier phases under the Climate Promise, as well as UNDP’s ongoing portfolio on renewable energy, climate-resilient agriculture, and just transition pathways. It draws on established models and lessons from prior initiatives that have focused on strengthening energy security, promoting renewable energy-based green technologies, and integrating smallholder farmers into resilient agricultural value chains particularly in vulnerable districts such as Kilinochchi and Nuwara Eliya. By scaling and deepening these proven approaches, the project is positioned within a broader, programmatic framework that 
supports Sri Lanka’s NDC implementation and long-term net-zero ambitions. As such, the Climate-Smart Dairy intervention is not a standalone effort but part of a coherent continuum of support, reinforcing inclusive, gender-responsive, and climate-resilient agricultural transformation while contributing to a just transition for rural communities. By establishing a Climate-Smart Dairy ecosystem, the intervention will reduce emissions, enhance dairy yields, and build adaptive capacity, supporting a just and inclusive transition toward a sustainable, climate-resilient dairy sector in Sri Lanka. 

Project expects to support, 
- Direct beneficiaries (number, men/women): 750 smallholder famers (400 women/350 men) and 100 government officers. 
- Indirect Beneficiaries: 5,000 (including family members, aspiring youth agri-entrepreneurs, veterinary officers, animal health professionals, local milk collectors & other community members)

projects.name: Gender Responsive Advancement and Operational Enhancement for Women Deminers in the Northern and Eastern Provinces of Sri Lanka (1005680)
projects.description:
Sri Lanka continues to face a significant landmine and unexploded ordnance (UXO) challenge in its Northern and 
Eastern Provinces, where contamination remains concentrated near communities, infrastructure, and productive 
land. The National Mine Action Centre (NMAC), established with UNDP support, leads national coordination and 
implementation under the Mine Action Strategy (2023–2027) in order to meet Sri Lanka’s obligations under the Anti-Personnel Mine Ban Convention. While notable progress has been achieved, newly identified hazardous areas, 
funding constraints, and increasingly complex operating conditions continue to place pressure on national clearance timelines and operational capacity. 
 
Women comprise approximately 30 percent of Sri Lanka’s demining workforce, one of the highest proportions 
globally, and play a critical role in sustaining mine action operations. Many women deminers are heads of households or primary income earners in conflict-affected communities. Despite their contribution, women deminers continue to face structural and operational challenges, including demanding field conditions, limited access to gender responsive equipment, and constraints on technical advancement within mine action operations. Ensuring safe, inclusive, and enabling working environments for women deminers is therefore essential to sustaining clearance progress and protecting livelihoods dependent on the sector. 
 
In addition, recent extreme weather events, including Cyclone Ditwah and associated flooding, have further complicated the mine action operating environment in parts of the Northern and Eastern Provinces. Heavy rainfall, 
flooding, and soil erosion have disrupted access to previously surveyed area, and increased the risk of mine and UXO re-exposure in areas thought to be safe. These climate-related impacts have introduced new operational 
uncertainties and intensified safety risks for deminers working in already challenging conditions.  
 
Against this backdrop, the National Mine Action Centre (NMAC) and its partners are prioritising rapid non-technical 
surveys, re-marking hazardous zones, and restoring damaged demining facilities, alongside Explosive Ordnance Risk Education (EORE) campaigns to protect affected communities. These efforts are vital to achieving Sri Lanka’s 2027 mine-free goal under the National Mine Action Completion Strategy, which is now facing delays due to climate induced recontamination and operational disruptions. 
 
In response to these efforts, the project will engage in (1) Identifying and deploying advanced demining technologies to support remapping of contaminated areas, increase clearance speed, precision and safety, (2) Supporting immediate operational needs through non-technical surveys to identify new hazardous areas, and Explosive Ordnance Risk Education (EORE) for at-risk communities to safeguard people in the post-disaster context. In the process, it will directly benefit approximately 2500 demining workers including 750 women deminers and indirectly benefit 10,000 people including families of the deminers. As such, it will enhance community resilience in post disaster, mine-affected environments through inclusive, safe, and dignified living and working conditions. 
 
While adopting an enabling approach to gender equality and social inclusion, the project focuses on physical systems, equipment, and facilities that allow deminers—especially women—to operate safely and efficiently in challenging conditions. Through these investments in tangible assets and field improvements, the project will strengthen national mine action capacity, support timely progress towards the 2028 clearance deadline, and contribute to safer, more inclusive, and climate-resilient mine action operations across Sri Lanka’s most affected regions.

Asia and Pacific countries are amongst the most vulnerable to climate change. The impacts of climate change are increasingly disrupting national economies and affecting livelihoods, water, energy, transportation, agriculture and ecosystems at an unprecedented scale. It is usually the poorest and the most vulnerable who are most at risk of the storms, floods, droughts, wildfires and rising sea levels, while lacking protections and resources to adapt. At the same time, here is growing recognition that affordable, scalable solutions are possible both for mitigation of greenhouse gas emissions and adaptation – and that these solutions can enable all of us to leapfrog to cleaner, more resilient economies. However, these call for policy and financing shifts away from business as usual to actively factor in climate change as well as ensure co-benefits and a focus on the needs of the most vulnerable.

projects.name: Refugee Health operations
projects.description:
This operation is primarily funded by USRAP (77.1%), Canada (8.2%) and New Zealand (14.7%). This received the termination letter from USRAP, so the 77.1% funding is cancelled.

The overall aim of this project is to facilitate safe and healthy migration by ensuring that applicants for USRAP meet the immigration health requirements, improve the health of USRAP beneficiaries, and to strengthen IOM's capacity to conduct health assessment services for approved refugees. Through this project, IOM Migration Health Assessment Centres (MHACs) will conduct or arrange health assessments, including vaccinations, for refugees in accordance with the immigration health guidelines of the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, Division of Global Migration and Quarantine (CDC/DGMQ) that are relevant for the country of operation (regulated by CDC/DGMQ’s: “Technical Instructions for Medical Examination of Aliens used by the Panel Physicians in the medical examinations conducted outside of the United States” and supplemental Guidance for Performing the Overseas Medical Examination of Refugees with Significant Medical Conditions”).

As part of the suite of Health Assessment (HA) activities, IOM MHACs will either facilitate referrals, or provide treatment directly to beneficiaries diagnosed with medical conditions that require follow-up for their appropriate medical treatment. Other activities under this project will serve to strengthen IOM’s ability to continue to provide quality HA through establishment of diagnostic facilities (i.e. laboratory and radiological capacities) or establish partnerships with pre-existing facilities in accordance with internationally accepted and IOM standards and maintain quality control for facilities.

projects.name: Promoting Participation Pathways for Human Development (01003844)
projects.description:
This project in Sri Lanka builds on ongoing efforts within the Sri Lankan Parliament and lessons from UNDP’s recently concluded initiative on strengthening local government capacities for inclusive development. It emphasizes creating stronger connections between national and sub-national engagement spaces to foster inclusive, participatory governance. Key interventions include strengthening public engagement in parliamentary oversight committees, optimizing the Parliament's Public Outreach and Media Departments, and developing tools and strategies for citizen participation in legislative impact assessment processes, both pre- and post-enactment.

The project will enhance the capacity of the Right to Information Commission, promoting public oversight, awareness, and access to parliamentary oversight functions. A critical component is the development of an online citizen engagement platform to enable dialogue between Parliament and the public, fostering participatory policymaking. Additionally, the initiative supports the creation of a civil society network, including the revival of Youth Peace and Security Coalitions, to advance dialogue on the regulatory framework for civic engagement. It will also develop mentorship initiatives and a comprehensive network of young and seasoned women leaders, creating an enabling environment for women aspiring to enter politics through skills development and resource support.

Globally, the initiative is designed to go beyond country-specific results by promoting cross-country knowledge exchange and collaboration, distilling national insights into global knowledge products, and leveraging interventions into global partnerships. Through the 3P4D initiative, the project will generate evidence on effective strategies for nurturing civic space, offering insights into technically sound and politically viable approaches. These lessons will be positioned and showcased to regional and global audiences, contributing to knowledge generation and advancing civic engagement as a strategic global objective.

projects.name: Support toward Selected Anti-Corruption Initiatives (01003869)
projects.description:
The project aims to enhance Sri Lanka's anti-corruption mechanisms through three strategic interventions. First, the development of an E-Asset Declaration System will transition the existing manual system to a digital platform, ensuring greater transparency, accessibility, and efficiency in compliance with the Right to Information Act (2016) and the Personal Data Protection Act (2022). This system will modernize asset declarations, making them more effective in detecting conflicts of interest and illicit wealth accumulation.

Moreover, a knowledge exchange visit to the Independent Commission Against Corruption (ICAC) in Hong Kong will provide CIABOC prosecutors and investigators with exposure to international best practices in corruption prevention, investigation, and prosecution. This initiative aims to strengthen institutional capacities by integrating successful strategies from ICAC into Sri Lanka’s anti-corruption framework.

Lastly, the project will conduct a Corruption Risk Assessment in Revenue Institutions, focusing on the Inland Revenue Department (IRD) and the Excise Department. This assessment will identify corruption vulnerabilities and recommend mitigation strategies to strengthen governance and institutional integrity in these key revenue-generating bodies.

Sri Lanka’s new anti-corruption law (2023) mandates the modernization of asset declaration processes and strengthens CIABOC's role in investigating and preventing corruption. The project directly supports these legal requirements while addressing persistent challenges such as inefficiencies in the manual asset declaration system and corruption risks within revenue institutions. Additionally, the knowledge exchange with ICAC ensures that CIABOC aligns its investigative and preventive approaches with international best practices.

The project will be implemented through a phased approach. The E-Asset Declaration System is expected to be developed by January 2025, with regulatory guidelines and user training incorporated into the rollout. The ICAC Knowledge Exchange Visit is scheduled for August 2025, focusing on hands-on training and strategic learning. The Corruption Risk Assessment and Mitigation Plans for revenue institutions will be conducted between January and March 2026, leading to the development of targeted action plans for corruption risk management.

By implementing these strategic interventions, UNDP aims to strengthen Sri Lanka’s anti-corruption framework, enhance transparency, and improve governance in revenue administration and public sector accountability.

projects.name: Strengthening Gender-Inclusive and Democratic Processes in Sri Lanka (ID 1000809)
projects.description: Sri Lanka’s governance crisis has worsened over the period 2020-2022. Weakened governance structures, perceived absence of accountability and incoherent planning across multiple political cycles and sectors have led to organic public unrest with people demanding a system change in the country. The country is also going through the worst economic crisis since independence. Given the current political and economic context in Sri Lanka, initiatives aimed at building public trust in public institutions, especially the Parliament, and positioning them as strong institutions within the democratic governance architecture, remain a key priority, especially in the area of public finance management. There is also a need to narrow the gender gap in governance, and address inequalities that prevent women from entering the highest levels of leadership in governance-related decision making. This needs to be achieved by promoting women’s entry into politics facilitated through public engagement, solidarity, evidence-led capacity building, strengthened collective voice and agency and sustained advocacy. Given the pressure on the country to improve public sector accountability, effectiveness and efficiency, there is a huge drive for improved economic governance with a focus on public sector reform (also in view of the IMF recommendations for debt restructuring and economic recovery in the long term). Given this contextual need, and building on the ongoing overall support to Sri Lanka in its governance spectrum, UNDP envisages focusing on three strategic areas: 1) improve capacities of the Parliament on all core functions (law-making, oversight, representation and budgetary) especially including on public finance management, public engagement, increased accountability, transparency and gender equality 2) strengthen stakeholder capacities and to secure buy-in for increased women's political participation, decision-making and access to leadership roles and 3) improve gender sensitive economic governance with a focus on public sector service delivery and public outreach for transparency and accountability.

projects.name: Kigali Implementation Plan - Stage I (1006010)
projects.description:
Sri Lanka, as a Party to the Montreal Protocol and all its amendments including the Kigali Amendment (2018), is committed to reducing the consumption of hydrofluorocarbons (HFCs), which are potent greenhouse gases used primarily in refrigeration and air-conditioning equipment. Under the Kigali Amendment, Sri Lanka is required to freeze HFC consumption at its baseline level and progressively reduce consumption by 80 per cent by 2045.

To support compliance with these obligations, Sri Lanka developed Stage I of its Kigali Implementation Plan (KIP) for the period 2025–2029. The plan aims to achieve a 10 per cent reduction in HFC consumption from the national baseline by 2029, equivalent to phasing down 117,023 tonnes of CO₂ equivalent HFCs. Key interventions focus on promoting low-global-warming-potential (GWP) alternatives in the refrigeration and air-conditioning (RAC) sector, strengthening policy and regulatory frameworks, enhancing technical capacity, and ensuring the safe adoption of alternative technologies while maintaining energy efficiency.

On behalf of the Government of Sri Lanka, the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP), as the lead implementing agency, submitted the Stage I KIP proposal to the 96th Meeting of the Executive Committee of the Multilateral Fund (MLF) held in Montreal from 26–30 May 2025. The Executive Committee approved, in principle, Stage I of the KIP for Sri Lanka with total funding of US$455,677, comprising US$325,307 for UNDP (including agency support costs) and US$130,370 for UNEP (including agency support costs), under Decision 96/45.

projects.name: Strengthening Risk-based Approaches to Border Security in Sri Lanka
projects.description:
Since 2016, the International Organization for Migration (IOM) has been supporting the Government of Sri Lanka (GoSL) to transition to a risk-based, intelligence-driven, well-coordinated approach to border management under an Integrated Border Management (IBM) model.  This project aims to consolidate these efforts by strengthening application of risk-based approaches to border security, thereby improving the capacities to facilitate legitimate travel and trade through Sri Lanka’s borders and mitigate vulnerabilities to transnational organized crime.  Towards this end, the project is structured around four critical components: improving risk-assessment capacities of the Sri Lanka border control authorities, enhancing screening of passengers and passenger goods at points of entry (PoE), improving border data management and analysis, and strengthening inter-agency coordination mechanisms through the Sri Lanka Border Risk Assessment Centre (BRAC).   
The project aims to enhance Sri Lanka Customs' capacity to screen passengers, goods, and courier packages in line with the Customs Ordinance[2]  by assessing current screening technologies at points of entry, identifying critical gaps, and procuring necessary screening equipment. Technical support to BRAC will focus on refining their data schema and revising system workflows with a view to enhancing data accuracy, process-efficiency, and monitoring, evaluating and reporting capabilities. To complement these efforts, a capacity building program will be implemented to strengthen the application of risk assessment principles within Sri Lanka Customs and BRAC and improve coordination among relevant risk management divisions. Collectively, these interventions aim to foster a culture of risk-based, coordinated approach to border security.
The capacity building programmes under the project will integrate human rights, diversity and gender considerations in the context of immigration and border governance in line with IOM values.
The anticipated outputs—enhanced screening capabilities at PoE, improved risk assessment capacities, and refined border data management practices—are expected to substantially contribute to the project's broader outcome of strengthened border security and the facilitation of legitimate travel and trade.

It will promote an integrated and coordinated framework for planning and managing ecosystems, engaging all sectors and local communities that impact or depend on these ecosystems. The intervention pathways include strengthening governance, policies, and institutional capacities for integrated landscape and seascape management, fostering financing and incentives for nature-positive practices, and demonstrating ecosystem-based management and nature-based solutions with potential for replication and scaling.

3: Piloting ecosystem and nature-based solutions to enhance environmental and economic benefits in selected coastal landscapes and seascapes.

4: Awareness raising, knowledge management, and gender mainstreaming to promote replication and scale-up of integrated approaches to resource management.

5: Monitoring and Evaluation.
Through these interventions, the project aims to strengthen ecosystem resilience, mitigate environmental threats, and promote sustainable economic pathways while ensuring inclusivity and long-term sustainability.

projects.name: Blue Economy Pipeline Development with a focus on Marine Tourism
projects.description:
For Sri Lanka, the Blue Economy offers a diverse range of opportunities for sustainable, clean, and fair growth in both traditional and emerging sectors, but it also requires innovation to meet these sustainability objectives. Leveraging the country’s vast ocean resources to advance ‘blue industries’ that supply goods and services to ‘blue value chains’ offer an innovative pathway to improve Sri Lanka’s external and trade balances. The pathway also provides an entry point to strengthen the equitable access of livelihood and economic opportunities for women and girls.

Adopting an integrated ‘blue economy’ approach – balancing both economic and conservation objectives - is aligned with UNDP’s Strategic Plan 2022-2025 and with the current Sri Lanka Country Programme. UNDP’s ambition is to support a blue economy that sustainably utilizes ocean resources for inclusive and sustainable development in Sri Lanka. This is also detailed in UNDP’s Ocean Promise and the integrated offer to Small Island Developing States (SIDS) – Rising Up for SIDS - which prioritizes climate action, blue economy acceleration, and digital transformation. 

Amongst other key priority areas within the blue economy, Sri Lanka’s marine tourism industry can evolve and unlock further opportunities for economic development and creation of ‘blue jobs’. By capitalizing on its natural resources, Sri Lanka can further drive economic growth and ensure the preservation of its marine environments for future generations.  

Against this backdrop, there are opportunities to put in place certain foundations to develop a pipeline of bankable 
projects focused on Sri Lanka’s blue economy.  

In this regard, UNDP Sri Lanka’s integrated service offer on blue tourism consists of 1) a blue economy development approach with a Marine Spatial Plan as the central governance framework, 2) collaboration with partners such as the Asian Development Bank (ADB) on marine tourism business models, 3) Northern and Eastern province tourism development, and other activities that are central to innovation in blue economy for sustainable growth.

The HIH is designed to address poverty reduction and is intrinsically linked to agri-food investment in several ways: 
•	Territorial approach: By identifying specific geographic and sectoral areas where the impact can be maximized, the initiative helps direct investments to where they are most needed.

•	Market Access: Improving infrastructure and logistics to provide farmers better access to markets is a key component, thus increasing their potential revenue and investment returns. 
•	Capacity Building: The initiative invests in training and equipping local communities and governments to manage agricultural projects effectively, ensuring long-term sustainability.

projects.name: Country enabled to address risk factors to prevent noncommunicable diseases (NCDs) through multi-sectoral actions.
projects.description: NCDs account for 83% of all adult deaths in Sri Lanka. Ischemic heart disease, stroke, neoplasms in hospital settings accounting for nearly 50% of deaths in 2021. Demographic transition, resulting in rapid aging of the population and unplanned urbanization and globalization of marketing and trade, leading to accumulation of multiple risk factors have been the main drivers behind this ‘epidemic’ of NCDs. National survey data from the Medical Research Institute clearly indicates a dramatic increase in overweight and obesity levels among children and adolescents. Sri Lanka has updated National Multisectoral Action Plan for the prevention and control of chronic Non-Communicable Diseases 2023-2027, as a continuation of strategies stipulated and the goals to reduce morbidity, disability, and premature mortality due to NCDs. The multisectoral action plan lays emphases on reducing the prevalence of key behavioural risk factors; tobacco use, alcohol intake, physical inactivity, and unhealthy diet, that are responsible for increasing trends of obesity, hypertension, diabetes, and resulting NCDs. WHO is supporting the Ministry of Health in accelerating and prioritizing actions to control risk factors. An Implementation Roadmap for accelerating the prevention and control of noncommunicable diseases in South-East Asia 2022–2030 (SEA/RC75/R2) adopted by the Regional Committee in September 2022 provides strategic directions to implement the most impactful interventions for risk factor reduction. WHO Sri Lanka will support activities with MOH, NATA and partner civil society organizations to advance implementation of specific interventions under key WHO technical intervention packages –  WHO MPOWER (for tobacco control under the WHO Framework Convention on tobacco control), WHO SHAKE (for salt reduction), and WHO REPLACE (for eliminating industrially produced trans-fatty acids), WHO ACTIVE (to improve physical activity) and WHO SAFER (to reduce use of alcohol) at national and subnational level.

projects.name: JI: Country enabled to address environmental determinants of health including WASH and climate change
projects.description: Climate change is affecting human health and health systems, including health infrastructure and health care services. The most impacted ones are the vulnerable populations with increasing poverties and inequities. projects.name: JI: Preparedness, readiness, response and resilience for health emergencies enhanced
projects.description:
Providing Psychological, Medical, and Reproductive Health Support to Refugees Residing in Sri Lanka" 
Objective:  To contribute to improved physical, mental, and social well-being of refugees and asylum seekers residing in Sri Lanka through improved access to healthcare services, medication, and health risk communication.   The project envisages the following outcome and outputs to achieve the objective:  

Outcome 1:   Refugees and asylum seekers enjoy better physical, mental, and social wellness.  

Output 1.1:     Refugees and asylum seekers have access to a multilingual 24/7 health hotline and are assisted to improve their physical, mental, and social well-being.  

Activities:      

1.1.1    Re-establish and operate the 24/7 IOM multilingual health hotline operated by an IOM nurse, and an on-call IOM physician.                         

1.1.2    Provide psychological support/counselling to refugees and asylum seekers through the 24/7 hotline.                         

1.1.3    Follow up on refugees and asylum seekers identified as having non-communicable diseases through the 24/7 hotline operated by an IOM nurse.                         

1.1.4   Provide reproductive health, maternal health, and child health advice to refugees and asylum seekers through the 24/7 hotline operated by an IOM nurse and facilitate referrals as necessary.                         

1.1.5   Follow up with refugees and asylum seekers admitted to government sector hospital facilities during and after hospital visits.                        

Under the project, IOM will re-establish the 24/7 multilingual health hotline services by mobilizing the existing IOM medical capacity.  With assistance of interpreters of multiple languages spoken by the refugees and asylum seekers, an IOM Nurse will provide health consultation services, facilitate their referral to government medical facilities and follow up to meet their primary health care needs, including mental health conditions, communicable and non-communicable diseases, reproductive health, maternal and child health, and hospital admission.  

Output 1.2:       Refugees and asylum seekers have access to essential medication.    

Activities:      

1.2.1   Provide essential medicine not available in government sector treating facilities to refugees and asylum seekers with chronic medical conditions, including in-patient care, through the UNHCR partner.                   

The project will deliver regular medication not available at the government medical facilities for chronic medical conditions, such as mental health conditions, hypertension, and diabetes. By assuring regular medications, the project also aims to reduce psychological distress and improve patient mental and physical well-being.  This intervention is not limited to outpatients but also serves patients admitted to hospital and who require essential medication.  

Output 1.3:      Refugees and asylum seekers have access to health risk communication messages and gain better knowledge on communicable and non-communicable diseases, reproductive health, maternal health, and child health.  

Activities:      

1.3.1   Provide periodic health risk communication messages in the local languages of refugees and asylum seekers through the health risk communication platform (WhatsApp broadcast) operated by IOM.                     

The project will develop health promotion materials and messages, and periodically disseminate health risk communication messages in the local languages of refugees and asylum seekers through a health risk communication platform (WhatsApp broadcast) operated by IOM.

(SRF) Outcome (Short-term Outcome 1a.1): Crisis-affected populations have their basic needs met and have minimum living conditions with reduced barriers to access for marginalized and vulnerable individuals.
